factual_claims.claim: Legal personhood has historically functioned as a flexible governance tool rather than a recognition of moral agency. It has been extended to entities like corporations, trusts, and rivers to manage liability and asset control.
The European Union withdrew its proposed AI Liability Directive in 2025 due to industry resistance and lack of political consensus. The EU has shifted toward a risk-based framework under the AI Act.
Corporate personhood was developed in the 19th century as an instrumental tool to facilitate large-scale industrial ventures and shield individual investors from unlimited liability.
The Te Awa Tupua Act 2017 in New Zealand granted legal personhood to the Whanganui River, recognizing it as a living entity with rights represented by appointed guardians.

The US Federal Circuit ruled in Thaler v Vidal (2022) that AI cannot qualify as a legal agent for intellectual property rights because inventorship requires a conscious, intentional act by a natural person.
The European Commission withdrew the proposed AI Liability Directive in its 2025 Work Programme due to insufficient political support and industry concerns regarding litigation risks.
Major global jurisdictions, including the EU, U.S., Canada, Brazil, Japan, South Korea, and China, have all rejected the concept of AI legal personhood.
The U.S. federal court system, specifically in Thaler v Vidal, has confirmed that legal personhood is exclusive to human agency.
The European Commission has shifted its regulatory approach away from standalone AI liability legislation toward a risk-based model under the AI Act.
